description: We’re Aanya and Aaira, two high-school students and best friends since birth. We’ve grown up side by side, sharing childhood memories, endless questions and a curiosity about the world. Aanya loves computer science, data science, maths and economics, especially finding meaning in data. Aaira is fascinated by Earth, space and planetary science. Our interests may be different, but growing up together has taught us how much we can discover when we combine them.
summary: How long must we watch before we know? Anyone can now plot NASA data in minutes. Far fewer can tell whether the line they see is a real trend or noise, and a result of "not significant" is usually read as "nothing is happening". The Long Watch is a web instrument that lets a student pick a place, ask a plain question, commit to a prediction, and then watch a real NASA record grow year by year. It marks the year a trend became statistically detectable, or estimates how many more years of observation would be needed. It turns statistical significance from a verdict into something a person can watch arrive.
details:
The Long Watch

Team Baseline: Aanya Sharma and Aaira Mustafa Raheem

How long must we watch before we know?

The problem

A graph can look convincing long before the evidence is.

When we look at environmental data, it's easy to see what appears to be a trend. Temperatures rise, rainfall changes, and air pollution seems to improve or worsen. But how do we know whether we're seeing a long-term change or ordinary variation in the data?

That question became the starting point for The Long Watch.

One problem is that environmental measurements aren't independent. What happens in one month is often related to the month before. Ordinary spreadsheet regression can overlook this relationship, making results appear more statistically convincing than they really are.

We tested this using simulated environmental records with no underlying trend. When autocorrelation was ignored, the tests incorrectly identified significant trends in 14–52% of cases, depending on the conditions.

That led us to another question: If a trend isn't statistically detectable yet, does that mean nothing is changing, or do we simply need more observations?

We wanted to investigate how the answer changes as an environmental record grows. Existing tools could plot the data and calculate a trend, but we couldn't find a public application that let users replay the development of statistical evidence across a NASA record in this way.

So we built one.

What we built and how it works

The Long Watch is an interactive web application that helps people investigate environmental change using real NASA Earth science data. We built it with a Python analysis service and a custom React interface.

We wanted users to take part in the investigation, rather than simply receive a graph and a conclusion.

Earth is the starting point: Users explore a globe built with NASA imagery, rotate and zoom into different regions, and select a location. The application retrieves its environmental record through NASA POWER and shows the actual geographic footprint of the data.

This matters because clicking on a city doesn't mean the dataset represents a measurement taken at that exact point. NASA's gridded records often represent much larger areas, and we wanted users to see what they were analysing.

Prediction comes before the results! Users choose whether they expect the variable to be rising, falling, or showing no detectable change. They make their prediction before seeing the data, giving them a reason to question what the results reveal.

Watch Replay is the heart of the application: Two charts move together along the same timeline. The first shows monthly departures from the regular seasonal cycle. The second shows the estimated rate of change and its 95% confidence interval.

As the replay advances, the statistics are recalculated using only observations available up to each historical endpoint. Users can watch the estimate change, the uncertainty evolve, and the evidence for a trend develop over time.

The application also identifies the earliest year from which detection remains sustained through the rest of the available record. This milestone is calculated retrospectively, using the completed record. It doesn't mean the future persistence of the result could have been known at that time.

An uncertain result leads to another investigation: When a trend isn't detected, The Long Watch estimates how much observational data might be needed to detect an assumed continuing trend with 90% probability.

Based on Weatherhead et al. (1998), the calculation considers the estimated rate, variability and autocorrelation. It also shows how the answer changes across the uncertainty interval. We deliberately avoid presenting this as a prediction of a future calendar year.

Every result can be checked: The application records its NASA source, retrieval details, preprocessing steps and statistical methods. Users can export an analysis, rerun it, and verify whether the reported values are reproduced.

What we discovered

We tested The Long Watch using actual NASA environmental records. Some results were straightforward. Others made us look more carefully at what the statistics were telling us.

One of our main investigations uses NASA's MERRA-2 data for Madrid, covering 1981–2025.

The air-temperature record shows a trend of +0.33 °C per decade, with a 95% interval from +0.21 to +0.45 °C per decade.

When we replay the full 45-year record, 2016 is the earliest historical endpoint from which the trend remains detected through every later year. Starting from 1981, that represents 36 years of observations. The milestone is identified in hindsight and depends on the chosen start year.

The precipitation record for the same grid cell produces a very different answer.

Its estimated trend is +0.03 mm/day per decade, with an interval from −0.03 to +0.10. Even with the same 45 years of observations, the trend is not statistically detected.

Under the fitted trend and noise assumptions, approximately 77 years of total observations would be needed for a 90% probability of detection at the estimated precipitation rate. At the stronger end of the rate interval, the existing record would already be long enough. At the weaker end, which includes zero, a meaningful detection length cannot be established.

There are also limitations to interpreting precipitation trends from reanalysis data, including possible artificial shifts.

What makes this comparison interesting is that both records come from the same grid cell and cover exactly the same years. Yet the statistical evidence is different.

The length of the record matters, but so do the strength of the trend, the variability around it, and the persistence of that variability.

We also investigated air pollution using tropospheric nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) records from NASA's OMI/Aura satellite.

New York shows a detectable long-term decline. The North China Plain has an overall falling trend, but an earlier period showed a detectable increase. In the Delhi region, a rising trend was detected during 2014–2020, but that detection did not remain sustained as more observations became available.

These cases revealed something important about Watch Replay: evidence doesn't always become stronger with each additional year. New observations can change the conclusion.

To select our demonstrations, we screened 22 cities across four environmental variables, producing 88 analyses.

Not every result matched our expectations. For example, the full-period MERRA-2 temperature record for Delhi showed no detectable linear trend. We investigated and documented that finding instead of excluding it because it was unexpected.

How we developed and tested it

We built the application using Python and React.

Python handles NASA data retrieval, preparation and statistical calculations. React powers the interactive globe, charts, controls and Watch Replay experience.

We worked with several NASA data products:

  • NASA POWER / MERRA-2: Monthly air temperature, precipitation and soil wetness, with records extending back to 1981.
  • CERES SYN1deg: Surface solar irradiance.
  • OMI/Aura OMNO2d version 004: Tropospheric NO₂ column data for three selected regions, obtained through NASA Giovanni.
  • NASA Blue Marble and Earth at Night: The geographic imagery used on the globe.

For trend analysis, we use Theil–Sen estimation, confidence intervals and two autocorrelation-aware significance tests. We also account for seasonal cycles, missing observations and differences between NASA products.

A major part of development was checking whether the statistical methods worked as expected.

We didn't want to assume that using established formulas automatically made our conclusions reliable.

We developed 75 automated tests and conducted Monte Carlo experiments using 1,000 simulated records per setting.

Across the tested configurations, our adjusted detection rule incorrectly identified trends in 3.2–5.4% of trendless records. Uncorrected tests produced false-positive rates of 14–52%.

The reported confidence intervals achieved coverage between 93.2% and 95.6%.

Testing also helped us find and correct two calibration problems. We checked that each historical replay uses only observations available at that endpoint, without accidentally introducing information from later years.

This was particularly important because the entire Watch Replay experience depends on showing how evidence actually develops through time.

What makes The Long Watch creative

We didn't invent a new statistical test. The methods behind our analysis are established, and other tools already allow people to plot NASA environmental records and calculate trends.

Our idea was to change how people experience the evidence behind those calculations.

Instead of only presenting a final trend estimate, The Long Watch lets users investigate how that estimate developed.

They make a prediction, choose a location, examine the record, and watch the statistical result evolve year by year. They can see why an apparent trend may remain uncertain and why additional observations sometimes change an earlier conclusion.

When a trend isn't detected, the investigation doesn't have to end there. Users can explore the conditional record length needed for detection and how uncertain that estimate may be.

The globe helps connect each result to the physical area represented by the NASA data, while the provenance and export features make the analysis open to inspection.

We wanted the statistics to be something users could explore and question themselves.

Who we built it for and why it matters

The Long Watch is intended for students, educators and anyone interested in understanding environmental change through real scientific data.

Most people have encountered graphs showing rising temperatures, changing rainfall or declining pollution. Fewer have had an opportunity to explore how scientists determine whether those patterns are statistically detectable.

We wanted to make that process accessible without removing the uncertainty that makes it scientifically meaningful.

A result labelled "not significant" can easily be misunderstood as proof that nothing is changing. In reality, the available record may be too variable, too short, or otherwise insufficient to support a clear trend conclusion.

The Long Watch gives users a way to investigate that difference.

It also helps explain why sustained Earth observation is valuable. Long, consistent records allow researchers to investigate changes that shorter datasets may not reveal reliably.

We haven't conducted formal user testing yet, so we can't claim a measured improvement in scientific understanding. Evaluating that would be an important next step.

For now, we've built a working application that allows people to examine these questions using NASA data and reproducible statistical analysis.

What we considered

One of our biggest challenges was deciding how to make the science understandable without making the answers sound more certain than they were.

We wanted someone without a background in statistics to follow the investigation, while still giving more experienced users enough information to examine the methods.

That meant making several deliberate choices.

We identify MERRA-2 as reanalysis rather than presenting its values as direct local measurements. We leave missing observations as gaps. We keep confidence intervals visible alongside trend estimates.

We also examine how results change when the analysis begins in a different year, since a single linear trend may hide periods of faster change, slower change or reversal.

There are limits to what the application can conclude. Detecting a trend doesn't establish its cause. Failing to detect one doesn't prove that nothing has changed. And a conditional record-length estimate cannot tell us exactly when a trend will become detectable in the future.

We wanted those limitations to be understandable parts of the experience.

Why we chose this project

Our team, Baseline, shares an interest in mathematics, data and scientific research.

We've always enjoyed looking more closely at questions that seem simple at first. With environmental data, we found that the interesting part wasn't always whether a graph went up or down. It was understanding how much confidence we could place in what we were seeing.

As we explored NASA records, we became interested in why some trends could be detected relatively quickly while others remained uncertain after decades. We also wanted to understand why a finding could appear statistically significant at one point and become less convincing when more observations were added.

That curiosity shaped The Long Watch.

We wanted to give people a way to experience how scientific evidence develops, using actual Earth science records and calculations they can inspect themselves.

The question we kept coming back to was:

How long must we watch before we know?
